title: Dennis Gets Divorced

jokes.text: Dennis leaves cab fare on the nightstand for his own wife, then realizes she already lives there
jokes.setup: Dennis has left cab fare on the nightstand three mornings in a row — a classic post-hookup dismissal move
jokes.punchline: Maureen points out they're married and she's already home, exposing that Dennis has been treating his wife like a one-night stand he's trying to get rid of
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional cold open joke. The comedic concept — that Dennis is so emotionally unavailable he treats his own wife like a stranger he wants to leave — is perfectly character-integrated. Only Dennis Reynolds would do this. The structure is tight: the audience figures it out at the same time Dennis does, which is a satisfying payoff. It immediately establishes the entire episode's premise with one behavioral detail.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: But there's cab fare on the nightstand.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: That's the third morning in a row you've done that.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: We're married.

jokes.text: "We're married, and that's cool. I'm psyched, dude." Dennis's hollow, clearly unconvincing enthusiasm
jokes.setup: Dennis is visibly processing the reality that his wife isn't leaving
jokes.punchline: His attempt at enthusiasm — 'I'm psyched, dude' — is comically hollow and unconvincing, the word 'dude' addressing his wife making it worse
jokes.explanation: The deflated 'I'm psyched, dude' is a funny line reading gag — the word 'dude' aimed at a wife is perfect Dennis. Character-specific but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: Oh, I don't work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, oh, okay. I just thought maybe you weren't going to work recently because we were going through a little bit of a honeymoon phase. But you're saying that you don't have a job.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: No job.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No job at all? Wow.

jokes.text: "Don't go snooping around too much... Don't look in those drawers." / "What's in those drawers?" / "My sex tapes."
jokes.setup: Dennis nervously warns Maureen not to snoop around because things have moved fast
jokes.punchline: The ominous drawers contain sex tapes — a perfect Dennis detail that is simultaneously creepy, self-aggrandizing, and reveals why he's nervous
jokes.explanation: This is very character-specific — Dennis having a drawer full of sex tapes that he guards jealously is exactly right. The 'Yeah' he adds after announcing it, apparently unbothered, is a good button. Fits perfectly into Dennis's established creepiness.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: All yours.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: All mine.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: All mine all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: All the time.

jokes.text: "You told me it was the phone bill, man. Of course I signed it."
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie he signed a prenup and should move on
jokes.punchline: Charlie explains he thought it was the phone bill — revealing his functional illiteracy and blind trust, which is why he signed without reading
jokes.explanation: Deep character integration: Charlie's illiteracy/naivety about financial documents is long-established show canon. The line 'of course I signed it' as a logical conclusion from his perspective is funny and sad simultaneously — peak Charlie Kelly comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't-don't look in those drawers.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: What's in those drawers?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: My sex tapes.

jokes.text: "When he hands me something to sign and it's about money and papers, I sign it." — Charlie's talking head
jokes.setup: Charlie defending himself in confessional
jokes.punchline: His stated policy for financial documents is to sign them without reading — delivered with complete sincerity as if this is reasonable
jokes.explanation: A compact, perfectly economical line. The talking-head format makes Charlie's sincerity land harder. This is a callback that adds dimension rather than just repeating the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You told me it was the phone bill, man. / Of course I signed it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why would you think that you needed to sign a phone bill.

jokes.text: Frank bathing himself in the bar sink because he has no home
jokes.setup: Mac asks why Frank is bathing in the sink
jokes.punchline: Frank has literally moved into Paddy's Pub because the marriage with Charlie displaced him — the bar sink is now his bathroom
jokes.explanation: Strong visual comedy — Frank Reynolds bathing in the bar sink is the kind of image that defines this show. It also efficiently communicates the Charlie-Frank domestic fallout without over-explaining it. Rewatch bonus because seeing Frank actually in the sink is funnier than the description.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: When he hands me something to sign and it's about money and papers, I sign it.

jokes.text: "Typical. This is so typical. My God, Dee, you clearly have something you want to say. So let's just get it over with."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are discussing his lack of prenup
jokes.punchline: Dennis spots Dee visibly bursting with something to say and preemptively calls her out, trying to control even the moment of his own humiliation
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Dennis's need to be in control even when he's the butt of the joke is well-established. Not exceptional but serves the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Charlie, gets health insurance and I get diddly-squat.

jokes.text: "Dee, are you seriously bragging about sleeping with a married man?"
jokes.setup: Dee has been proudly listing her gifts from a married man
jokes.punchline: Mac's disbelief that she's bragging about it, naming the obviously wrong behavior she's been celebrating
jokes.explanation: Functional straight-man line. Mac voicing the audience's reaction is the structural purpose here rather than a genuinely clever joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Because I don't have a home anymore. So this is where I take a shower. This is where I live, Dennis.

jokes.text: "Yeah, one second you're on your high horse about how great marriage is, and now you're destroying one?"
jokes.setup: Dee has been defending marriage while simultaneously benefiting from an affair
jokes.punchline: Mac's pointed observation that she's doing both simultaneously and doesn't see the contradiction
jokes.explanation: Competent hypocrisy callout. Gets the job done.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, one second you're on your high horse about how great marriage is, and now you're destroying one?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not the one who's married. I didn't do anything wrong.

jokes.text: "Well, Frank, I'm not going to go passing on free cars."
jokes.setup: Frank points out Dee accepted a car from a married man
jokes.punchline: Dee's defense is completely amoral and pragmatic — she's not denying wrongdoing, just explaining her calculus
jokes.explanation: Very economical line that perfectly captures Dee's self-serving amorality. The straightforwardness of the defense is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Guys, guys, guys, guys, guys, all this talk about marriage and Dee being such a whore has got me thinking... I never got a bachelor party.

jokes.text: "Guys, guys, all this talk about marriage and Dee being such a whore has got me thinking... I never got a bachelor party."
jokes.setup: An earnest group discussion about the ethics of marriage and infidelity
jokes.punchline: Charlie's non-sequitur pivot — connecting 'marriage and Dee being such a whore' as one unified thought that somehow leads him to bachelor party grievances
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The construction is excellent: 'all this talk about marriage and Dee being such a whore' treats two very different things as equivalent inputs to his thought process, then the 'has got me thinking' misdirection sets up the absurd bachelor party pivot. The phrase 'Dee being such a whore' as a casual passing clause is peak Charlie obliviousness. Highly quotable, great character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Being married to Charlie's got me all confused. I got to get my hetero on.

jokes.text: "Being married to Charlie's got me all confused. I got to get my hetero on."
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining why he wants to go to a strip club
jokes.punchline: Mac admits his domestic partnership with Charlie has confused his sexuality — a winking acknowledgment of his closeted status that the show has been building for seasons
jokes.explanation: Deep character integration — Mac's suppressed homosexuality is a long-running thread. 'Get my hetero on' is a funny phrase, and the admission that Charlie has 'confused' him is funnier still. Rewatch bonus for audiences who know Mac's arc.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I like that move. What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's it. Motorcycle?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's pretty... Yeah, not like that, though. It's pretty good, but you got to use... a little bit more shoulder.

jokes.text: The guys at the strip club arguing about the correct way to do a 'motorcycle' dance move
jokes.setup: The gang is at a strip club for a bachelor party, ostensibly to have fun
jokes.punchline: They immediately get distracted by a pedantic argument about the correct shoulder technique for a dancing motorcycle impression — completely ignoring the actual strip club
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny behavioral comedy — the gang's inability to just enjoy anything without it becoming an argument. The specificity of 'more shoulder' as a correction is funny. The fact that they're doing this in a strip club makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Now do I write the word 'too' or should I write the number two? What's the best way to do that when we're texting back and forth?

jokes.text: "Now do I write the word 'too' or should I write the number two? What's the best way to do that when we're texting back and forth?"
jokes.setup: Dennis receives a 'miss you' text from Maureen and responds — a mundane texting moment
jokes.punchline: Dennis is paralyzed by the too/2 dilemma and treats it as a serious question for his friends at the strip club, revealing his absurd self-seriousness about everything
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny character detail — Dennis treating trivial things with enormous gravity. Not his strongest material but the bathos of worrying about spelling at a strip club is amusing.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: Sorry. You have to be a couple for that.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We are a couple.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: documents.

jokes.text: "Excuse me. Hi. What is the recommended amount of money for one to make it rain?" Dennis formally asking the stripper
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are debating whether Frank should make it rain
jokes.punchline: Dennis resolves the debate by formally consulting the stripper as if she's a maître d', asking for the 'recommended amount' — his pomposity applied to the most inappropriate context
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke — Dennis's formality and need to do things 'correctly' even in this context is very him. Asking a stripper for the 'recommended amount' as if consulting a sommelier is a great image. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm tightening the purse strings on this relationship until there's a little bit of give and take.

jokes.text: "How much would it cost for this gentleman and I to get a nice couple's dance?" Charlie asking on behalf of himself and Mac
jokes.setup: They are at a bachelor party, ostensibly to establish their heterosexuality
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately tries to book a couple's dance for himself and Mac — completely undermining the stated purpose of the trip
jokes.explanation: Great callback payoff — Mac just said he needed to get his hetero on, and within minutes Charlie is asking for a couple's dance for the two of them. Tight structure and excellent character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: 'Miss you more.' That's classic Maureen right there. She's always got to one-up me 'Miss you most.' Most... can't get more than most, right? So that should... that should be the end of it, right?

jokes.text: "Sorry. You have to be a couple for that." / "We are a couple." / "Charlie, documents."
jokes.setup: Charlie and Mac are denied the couple's dance
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately claims they ARE a couple, and Mac's response is not denial but 'documents' — meaning he wants Charlie to prove it with their marriage paperwork
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Documents' is an instantly iconic single-word punchline. Mac doesn't deny being a couple — he just wants the proof. The word choice 'documents' is unexpected, formal, and perfectly captures both Mac's earnestness and the absurdity of a married gay couple using their marriage certificate to get a couple's dance at a strip club. Extremely quotable and rewatchable.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Actually, I came clean to my wife. And she kicked me out of the house.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Ew. Ouch.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah. Bet you wish you could take that one back.

jokes.text: "I'm tightening the purse strings on this relationship until there's a little bit of give and take." Frank withholding money from Mac
jokes.setup: Frank has a money bag to make it rain; Mac wants some money
jokes.punchline: Frank talks about 'give and take' in the relationship while literally clutching his purse at a strip club — treating their friendship like a financial negotiation
jokes.explanation: Decent Frank moment. The 'purse strings' pun with an actual purse is a mild visual/wordplay gag, but not particularly inspired.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Dee, I gave you a car.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're gonna jam the car in my face, huh?

jokes.text: "Miss you more." / "That's classic Maureen right there. She's always got to one-up me." / "Miss you most." / "Most... can't get more than most, right? So that should be the end of it."
jokes.setup: Dennis is trading 'miss you' texts with Maureen and narrating them live
jokes.punchline: Dennis turns a sweet texting exchange into a competitive game he's trying to win, and is genuinely relieved when 'most' shuts it down — he's being competitive about affection
jokes.explanation: Very good character joke — Dennis treating 'miss you' as a competition he needs to win, then treating 'most' as a logical endpoint, is perfect Dennis narcissism. His relief that 'most' closes it out is a funny button.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: That is not your room anymore. It is my craft studio, so kindly stay out of there.

jokes.text: "Once you pop, you can't stop, am I right?" Dee making a Pringles joke about Bill showing up uninvited
jokes.setup: Bill Ponderosa has shown up at Dee's door having come clean to his wife and been kicked out
jokes.punchline: Dee jokes that he 'can't stop' (Pringles slogan) rather than engaging with his crisis
jokes.explanation: Weak joke. The Pringles reference is a lazy pop culture drop that doesn't really work — 'once you pop you can't stop' doesn't map cleanly onto this situation. It's the kind of joke a character makes when the writer needs them to seem glib but hasn't found a good line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She turned it into her craft studio where she makes terrible sweatshirts out of cats or... puts cats in sweatshirts

jokes.text: "She froze my assets." / "Yikes. / "Shit's getting pretty real for you, huh?"
jokes.setup: Bill explains he can't stay in a hotel because his wife froze his assets
jokes.punchline: Dee's response 'Shit's getting pretty real for you, huh?' is completely detached sympathy — she's narrating his crisis as an observer rather than showing any concern
jokes.explanation: Decent Dee moment — her detached commentary on other people's suffering is a character trait. 'Shit's getting pretty real' as cold analysis works.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't love you, Maureen. I don't love you. I never loved you. You're annoying and you're strange.

jokes.text: "Dee, I gave you a car." / "You're gonna jam the car in my face, huh?" / "Come in."
jokes.setup: Dee has firmly said she doesn't want Bill in her space and lists alternatives
jokes.punchline: Bill simply mentions the car, and Dee immediately capitulates — her entire moral stance dissolves for a car she already has
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure and economy. Dee's 'you're gonna jam the car in my face, huh?' shows she KNOWS what's happening, and then 'come in' shows she doesn't care. The two-word capitulation is perfect. The joke is in Dee's complete self-awareness combined with total lack of willpower.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's like her breath... Ugh! It's like always so bad. It's like a dead tooth. It's the dead tooth. I'm saying it now. I'll say it. You have a dead tooth.

jokes.text: Dennis arriving drunk at 2 AM blasting 'The Boys Are Back in Town' — the song playing him home triumphantly
jokes.setup: Dennis has been out all night for his bachelor party
jokes.punchline: He arrives home at 2 AM clearly wasted, with 'The Boys Are Back in Town' as his theme music — the triumphant song choice undercuts how pathetic the actual arrival is
jokes.explanation: Good visual/music joke. The triumphant classic rock arrival cutting to Maureen waiting in the apartment is a nice structural beat. Rewatch bonus for the visual of Dennis's smug entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah? How about if you guys don't leave, I call the cops and I tell 'em you beat me?

jokes.text: "No, I don't drink. You know that. I think it makes people look ugly."
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Maureen she's up now so they might as well do shots
jokes.punchline: Maureen's refusal — she doesn't drink because she thinks it makes people look ugly — is delivered as a sincere personal philosophy, oblivious to the irony of her appearance
jokes.explanation: Decent dark joke about Maureen's self-image vs. Dennis's (and the audience's) perception of her. The show has established Maureen as strange-looking; her vanity about drinking is funny in that context.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, shit, that's from... that's from Fear, dude. Oh, that's Marky Mark. That's Marky Mark. That's what Marky Mark does.

jokes.text: "That is not your room anymore. It is my craft studio, so kindly stay out of there."
jokes.setup: Dennis drunkenly heads toward his room
jokes.punchline: Maureen has already converted his room into a craft studio — she's been there for a brief time and already claimed territory
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of Dennis's nightmare domesticity — she's moved in and already redecorated. Sets up the following reveal about the cat sweatshirts.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Sorry. Want to have sex?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What?! No, no! God, no! Please close your legs up.

jokes.text: "She turned it into her craft studio where she makes terrible sweatshirts out of cats or... puts cats in sweatshirts"
jokes.setup: Dennis explains the craft studio to Mac
jokes.punchline: The craft is making cat sweatshirts — but Dennis can't even articulate whether the cats are in the sweatshirts or the sweatshirts are made OF cats, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist detail. The ambiguity Dennis introduces ('sweatshirts out of cats OR puts cats in sweatshirts') is a funny addition — his drunken confusion accidentally makes the image more disturbing. Good character establishment for Maureen as the show's weirdest recurring character.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: I don't give a shit about the car, okay? My life is in ruins. I'm gonna lose my kids.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Okay, great, so we're in agreement. I keep the car.

jokes.text: "I'm not entirely certain that Maureen Ponderosa..." Dennis trailing off mid-divorce threat, unable to finish
jokes.setup: Dennis begins to threaten divorce, addressing Maureen by her full name as if delivering a legal declaration
jokes.punchline: He loses his train of thought entirely mid-sentence — the grand divorce declaration becomes an incomplete mumble
jokes.explanation: Funny drunken pomposity gag. Dennis starting with 'Maureen Ponderosa' as if he's a lawyer and then completely trailing off captures drunk people's false confidence well.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: I don't give a shit about the car, okay? My life is in ruins. I'm gonna lose my kids.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Okay, great, so we're in agreement. I keep the car.

jokes.text: "Divorce! / What? What did you just say? / I will divorce you, Maureen. I'll do it."
jokes.setup: Dennis's first attempt at threatening divorce fizzled
jokes.punchline: He course-corrects by just yelling 'Divorce!' then delivering it formally — 'I will divorce you, Maureen. I'll do it.' like he's threatening a toddler
jokes.explanation: Good drunk escalation. The 'I'll do it' tacked on — as if she might not believe he means it — is a nice detail. Dennis threatening divorce like a petulant child rather than an adult is on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You think it's gonna be that easy, dude?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, yeah, of course. I mean, marriage and divorce these days, it's like a, it's more of a formality than anything else, you know?

jokes.text: "Okay, you're drunk. Why don't we just go to bed?" / "I'm not drunk. I'm more sober than I've ever been." / "Okay, I'm a little bit drink." / "I'm totally drunk, but my mind is sober."
jokes.setup: Maureen calls Dennis drunk; he denies it
jokes.punchline: His denial escalates through several stages — 'more sober than I've ever been' → 'a little bit drink' → 'totally drunk, but my mind is sober' — each one walking back the last while still asserting clarity
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the three-stage walk-back is well-constructed. 'A little bit drink' is a great malapropism, and 'my mind is sober' as the final Hail Mary is both a real thing drunk people say and a funny line. Highly quotable. One of the episode's stronger pure joke constructions.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Nobody washes the dishes! We eat the food directly off the coffee table, and you know it!

jokes.text: "I don't love you, Maureen. I never loved you. You're annoying and you're strange."
jokes.setup: Dennis declares he is 'sober of mind' and therefore what follows is genuine
jokes.punchline: The genuine revelation is that he doesn't love her, never did, and she's annoying and strange — delivered with the gravity of a dramatic TV confession
jokes.explanation: Dark character comedy — Dennis's sociopathic honesty is the show's core premise. 'You're annoying and you're strange' as his sincere explanation is bluntly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's coming up here. This... yeah, this is it right here. The Ponderosas' ponderosa.

jokes.text: "It's like her breath... Ugh! It's like always so bad. It's like a dead tooth. It's the dead tooth. I'm saying it now. I'll say it. You have a dead tooth."
jokes.setup: Dennis has just declared he doesn't love Maureen
jokes.punchline: He escalates to a specific physical complaint — her dead tooth breath — and builds himself up to saying it as if it's a great act of courage, 'I'll say it'
jokes.explanation: Very good cringe escalation. The specific detail of 'the dead tooth' is excellent — it's precise, disgusting, and petty. Dennis working himself up to say it as if it's a brave act ('I'll say it. I'm saying it now.') while Maureen stands there is great cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Kelly
dialogue.line: I know they're very small. It's been very hard on me.

jokes.text: "I'm the boy toy! You're my boy toy."
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Maureen to get her 'boy toy' out of his apartment, referring to Bill
jokes.punchline: Bill protests that he is not Maureen's boy toy — she is HIS boy toy — revealing his pathetic fixation on status even while being kicked out of a stranger's apartment
jokes.explanation: Good quick joke. Bill's insistence on the distinction — in this powerless moment — is funny. The repetition and reversal are nicely economical.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You can have the hot plate.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Hot dog!

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Now we're cooking with gas.

jokes.text: Maureen bruising herself on the wall, referencing the movie Fear — Dennis and Mac recognizing the Marky Mark move
jokes.setup: Maureen threatens to call the police and say Dennis beat her
jokes.punchline: She demonstrates by slamming herself against the wall — and Dennis and Mac immediately recognize it as the move from the movie Fear with Mark Wahlberg
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best set pieces. The concept is both dark (staging domestic violence evidence) and absurdist (learned from a 90s teen thriller). The fact that Dennis and Mac immediately recognize the specific movie move — 'That's what Marky Mark does!' — and start excitedly recapping the plot instead of being horrified is perfect Always Sunny. The escalation from threat to demonstration to film nerds is excellently structured.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: All I'm seeing is a series of drawings of elephants.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah. Well, Charlie did the elephant drawings.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, but... You should keep 'em.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I did those for you, man.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God! You are really making yourself at home here, huh?" / "Sorry. Want to have sex?"
jokes.setup: Dee returns home to find Bill Ponderosa fully at home in her space
jokes.punchline: His immediate pivot from apology to 'Want to have sex?' — delivered as a genuine offer, not a joke
jokes.explanation: Quick functional gag. The two-word pivot is economical. Bill's brazenness in proposing sex while crashing at her place is a decent character beat.

dialogue.line: If I didn't know any better, I'd say there's a lot of love in this room here.

jokes.text: "My life is in ruins." / "Mm-hmm." / "I'm gonna lose my kids." / "Okay, great, so we're in agreement. I keep the car."
jokes.setup: Bill is confessing the full horror of his situation — his family is destroyed
jokes.punchline: Dee interprets his resignation as agreement that she keeps the car — she has been tracking only her own interests throughout his entire emotional spiral
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Bill's genuine despair ('I'm gonna lose my kids') is immediately followed by Dee's purely transactional 'Okay, great, so we're in agreement.' The word 'great' as a response to 'I'm gonna lose my kids' is the dark comedy money shot. Highly economical, deeply character-integrated, and funny on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why did we have to do all the touching and the hand-holding if it was just...?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It was fun.

jokes.text: "Okay, well, then I'm gonna need the car to get over there." / "Okay, well, the car's off the table, okay? We just discussed the car."
jokes.setup: Dee tells Bill to go back to his wife
jokes.punchline: He immediately demands the car to do so, reopening the car negotiation she just closed — the car becomes a recurring point of absurd contention
jokes.explanation: Decent running gag extension. Dee's exasperated 'we just discussed the car' is good, but it's a diminishing return on the previous stronger joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I just kidnapped Bill Ponderosa's kids.

jokes.text: "Marriage and divorce these days is more of a formality than anything else... it's just sort of something that you do, right?" — Dennis's delusional optimism
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining to Charlie and Mac that his divorce will go smoothly
jokes.punchline: His completely unfounded confidence — 'of course, I mean, marriage and divorce is more of a formality' — coming from someone who just experienced a terrifying confrontation with his wife is classic Dennis delusion
jokes.explanation: Dennis's post-Fear-incident optimism about divorce being 'just a formality' is a good character beat — his ability to compartmentalize disaster into confidence is a Dennis hallmark. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I just kidnapped Bill Ponderosa's kids.

jokes.text: "'How did my laundry get so clean? Oh, who washed all the dishes today?' Nobody washes the dishes! We eat the food directly off the coffee table, and you know it!"
jokes.setup: Charlie is defending his contributions to the household
jokes.punchline: His examples of household contributions are so basic that Frank refutes them — they don't even use dishes, they eat off the coffee table, making Charlie's claimed domestic contributions impossible
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quotable jokes. It's deeply character-integrated — Frank and Charlie's feral domestic arrangement (eating off the coffee table, no dishes) is an established show detail, and using it to blow up Charlie's self-defense is perfect. The image of them eating directly off a coffee table is both disgusting and funny, and 'you know it!' as an accusation is a great button. This is the kind of specific, earned show mythology that elevates Always Sunny above generic dark comedy.

dialogue.line: All right, are the kids confined in any way, maybe in a crawl space or a backyard bunker?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: No, they're out in the car.
Have you touched them yet?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

jokes.text: "I'm gonna pull the plug. / You gonna flush our marriage down the toilet?! / Right down the toilet! / Flush it, big boy! / Yes, there he goes! Flush it down the toilet 'cause I don't care!"
jokes.setup: Frank threatens to end the marriage
jokes.punchline: The 'flush the marriage' metaphor escalates into both characters enthusiastically embracing the toilet imagery, with Charlie egging Frank on — 'flush it, big boy!'
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — the mutual enthusiasm for the toilet metaphor is funny, especially 'flush it, big boy' as Charlie's encouragement. The two of them essentially agreeing while ostensibly fighting is classic Frank/Charlie dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I tell you what, I did not mean to kidnap them. That was all... that was all this guy.

jokes.text: "We'll get that idiot lawyer that always helps us out. He does good by us." / "Yeah, he's excellent." / "But he slapped a restraining order on us, so we can't use him."
jokes.setup: They discuss getting their usual lawyer
jokes.punchline: Their lawyer — whom they both praise enthusiastically — has a restraining order against them, which they mention as a minor logistical obstacle rather than a red flag about their behavior
jokes.explanation: Very good joke structure — the enthusiastic praise of the lawyer ('excellent') immediately followed by the restraining order is well-timed. The gang treating a restraining order as a minor scheduling conflict is perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Bill's wife
dialogue.line: How much does he owe you?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Bill's wife
dialogue.line: How much does he owe you for the sex?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, no, no, no, no, no, no. I'm not a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Bill's wife
dialogue.line: Oh, well, congratulations. You're the only woman he didn't have to pay to sleep with.

jokes.text: "Is it you? Is it? 'Cause if it's you, I'm not interested."
jokes.setup: Frank says he thinks he knows someone who can take both their cases as a lawyer
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately suspects Frank IS the lawyer and preemptively rejects him — suggesting this exact scam has been attempted before
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Charlie's preemptive 'is it you?' suggests Frank has pulled this kind of scheme before. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Bill's Wife
dialogue.line: How much does he owe you for the sex?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, no, no, no, no, no, no. I'm not a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Bill's Wife
dialogue.line: Oh, well, congratulations. You're the only woman he didn't have to pay to sleep with.

jokes.text: "The Ponderosas' ponderosa." Dennis naming the Ponderosa house
jokes.setup: They pull up to Maureen's family home to drop Bill off
jokes.punchline: Dennis names the house 'The Ponderosas' ponderosa' — a reference to the TV show Bonanza's ranch while also literally describing the family name applied to their home
jokes.explanation: Smart wordplay — the Ponderosa family living in a 'ponderosa' (the TV ranch) is a clever double reference. Economical and shows some wit. Understated delivery makes it land as a quick gag.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's uncle
dialogue.line: Well, when I heard you were getting divorced, I-I felt compelled to involve myself.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, how would you have heard that I was getting a...

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's uncle
dialogue.line: I was listening to you drunkenly explain all that at 3:00 a.m.

jokes.text: Dee calls Dennis from outside the Ponderosa house; he thinks she's Maureen and starts the conversation warmly
jokes.setup: Dennis's phone rings; the audience expects it to be Maureen since he's been texting her
jokes.punchline: It's Dee — but his initial warm, domestic-partner tone makes the mundane sibling phone call much stranger
jokes.explanation: Mild misdirection joke — the 'Maureen?' / 'No it's Dee' beat is functional but not especially sharp. It works mainly as a scene transition device.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: The pleasure is all mine.
It's a pleasure to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: The pleasure's... still...

jokes.text: Dee on the phone, pretending to be Maureen while also managing her own car situation with Bill Ponderosa
jokes.setup: Dennis calls who he thinks is Maureen at the Ponderosa house
jokes.punchline: It's Dee — she has driven Bill's car to the house and is now entangled in the whole situation she was supposedly resolving
jokes.explanation: Decent structural comedy — Dee's presence at the house when Dennis calls creates a nice coincidental tangle. Not executed with great sharpness but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's uncle
dialogue.line: I use shea butter. Assorted lanolin products.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's uncle
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm serious, you could be a hand model. You've got the goods.

jokes.text: "I do love the car. Hands-free Blue... I can do all kinds of stuff with both hands."
jokes.setup: Dee is describing having 'let her guy go' as if it was a noble act
jokes.punchline: She immediately pivots to raving about the Bluetooth in the car she kept — her 'letting go' was just keeping his car and kicking him out
jokes.explanation: Good Dee character moment — her moral framing of 'letting him go' instantly revealed as self-serving. The pivot to praising the Bluetooth is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's uncle
dialogue.line: And you also acquired Ms. Ponderosa's debt.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Whoo-hoo.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What? You're in debt?

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: Not anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's uncle
dialogue.line: But you are... about 90K.

jokes.text: "Okay, hop in there." / "No! Wha-wha-wha-what is this?! What are you doing?" Dennis pushing Bill out of the car toward the angry wife
jokes.setup: Dee told Dennis to handle it; Dennis just wants this resolved
jokes.punchline: Dennis unceremoniously shoves Bill toward his furious wife — treating him like a package being delivered — and then panics when the wife approaches
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works in context. Dennis's total lack of sensitivity — just shoving Bill at the problem — and then fleeing is consistent character behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Uncle Jack, what the hell?!

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: I froze up.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: He's great.

jokes.text: "I'm so glad you called, Charlie. Your uncle never hears from you anymore." / "Well, you're kind of the only actual lawyer I know that doesn't have a restraining order against me. So I sort of had to call you."
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack (a lawyer with conspicuously small hands) is pleased Charlie called
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately deflates the warmth — he called because every other lawyer has a restraining order against him, not out of affection
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the restraining order setup. Charlie's brutal honesty — 'I sort of had to call you' — is funny and character-specific. Uncle Jack's small hands are a running gag that pays off throughout this scene.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: And would it be okay if you put your hands on top of mine? Like they're my hands?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Sure, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Like that?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Okay. That looks like my hands.

jokes.text: "Uh... with the touching, with the touching... none of that." / "You're put off by my hands. I know they're very small. It's been very hard on me."
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack greets Charlie warmly with his hands
jokes.punchline: Charlie recoils from his touch — Uncle Jack interprets this as being about his conspicuously small hands, which he's clearly sensitive about and brings up unprompted
jokes.explanation: Good character introduction of Uncle Jack. The small hands as his defining trait/insecurity is well-deployed here. 'It's been very hard on me' about hand size is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Kelly
dialogue.line: And would it be okay if you put your hands on top of mine? Like they're my hands? That looks like my hands.

jokes.text: "Don't let the dog off the leash, okay? Remember, the bigger man walks away first." / Charlie immediately capitulates: "You can have the hot plate." / "Hot dog! Now we're cooking with gas."
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack tells them to stay calm; the first item of contention is a hot plate
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately gives up the hot plate at Uncle Jack's first suggestion, and Uncle Jack celebrates with 'Hot dog! Now we're cooking with gas!' — an inadvertent hot food pun in a hot plate dispute
jokes.explanation: Good layered joke — Uncle Jack's food-based idioms ('hot dog,' 'cooking with gas') accidentally aligning with the hot plate dispute is a nice structural coincidence. Charlie's instant capitulation vs. his earlier fighting is funny character inconsistency.

jokes.text: "Moving along to art holdings. All I'm seeing is a series of drawings of elephants."
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack is cataloguing their shared assets like a formal divorce proceeding
jokes.punchline: Their only 'art holdings' are Charlie's elephant drawings — the formal legal language ('art holdings') applied to amateur elephant sketches is the joke
jokes.explanation: Very good absurdist moment. 'Art holdings' for Charlie's elephant drawings is perfect — the gap between formal legal language and the actual content is well-calibrated. It's also genuinely sweet, setting up the following exchange.

jokes.text: "Well, Charlie did the elephant drawings." / "Yeah, but... You should keep 'em." / "I did those for you, man." / "I like 'em." / "Well, you should like 'em. I put a lot of work into 'em." — Frank and Charlie having a genuine moment over elephant drawings
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack tries to adjudicate the elephant drawings
jokes.punchline: Frank and Charlie start tenderly negotiating over the elephant drawings and complimenting each other — in the middle of a contentious divorce — revealing genuine affection underneath their chaos
jokes.explanation: One of the most character-rich moments in the episode. The Frank/Charlie relationship is the show's dark heart — these two terrible people genuinely care for each other. The elephant drawings as a vessel for that affection is both funny and strangely touching. 'Well, you should like 'em. I put a lot of work into 'em.' is funny precisely because Charlie's self-satisfaction is real. This earns its high score through deep character integration and tonal complexity.

jokes.text: "If I didn't know any better, I'd say there's a lot of love in this room here."
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie just had a genuinely sweet moment over elephant drawings
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack narrates what the audience is also feeling — these two were just screaming at each other about flushing their marriage down the toilet, and now there's real warmth
jokes.explanation: Decent button on the previous moment. Uncle Jack articulating the irony is functional but slightly over-explains what was more effective left unspoken.

jokes.text: "Sounds like what you guys want is an annulment. It would essentially void your partnership." / "Yeah, right, that sounds perfect. Marriage blows." / "Preaching to the choir, fellas."
jokes.setup: They want to get back to their previous living arrangement
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack — a family lawyer — adds 'preaching to the choir' suggesting his own marriage is terrible, then swiftly pivots to the annulment paperwork
jokes.explanation: Decent quick gag. Uncle Jack's 'preaching to the choir' adds a character dimension efficiently.

jokes.text: "Why did we have to do all the touching and the hand-holding if it was just..." / "It was fun."
jokes.setup: The annulment was just two signatures; Charlie questions why there was so much physical contact from Uncle Jack
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack: 'It was fun.' — He made them hold hands and touch simply for his own enjoyment, not for any legal purpose
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and character integration. The implication that Uncle Jack manufactured legal-touching requirements purely for his own enjoyment is both dark and absurd. 'It was fun' as a two-word explanation — delivered as sufficient justification — is a great punchline. The small-hands running gag pays off here: he needed them to hold hands so he could enjoy the contact. Very rewatchable.

jokes.text: "Hey, Mac. Do you mind snapping a photo for the Web site? But keep my hands out of the shot."
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack is a lawyer who is deeply self-conscious about his small hands
jokes.punchline: He wants a photo for his law firm website but specifically requests his hands be excluded — his professional image requires hiding his hands
jokes.explanation: Great running gag payoff. The website photo request with the hands caveat is funny on its own and funnier as a callback. Uncle Jack as a character is efficiently established through this recurring element.

jokes.text: "I just kidnapped Bill Ponderosa's kids." / "All right, are the kids confined in any way, maybe in a crawl space or a backyard bunker?"
jokes.setup: Dennis calls Mac with news
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to 'I kidnapped some kids' is not horror but tactical clarification — asking if they're in a crawl space or bunker as if assessing the severity of a minor logistical problem
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and arguably the season. Mac's response — not 'what?!' but a calm, specific checklist of child confinement options — perfectly encapsulates the show's premise that these people are casually monstrous. 'Crawl space or backyard bunker' as the specific options Mac has apparently thought about is extraordinary dark comedy. The economy is perfect: two specific options deliver an entire character portrait. This is exactly the kind of joke that makes Always Sunny distinctive.

jokes.text: "No, they're out in the car." / "Have you touched them yet?" / "Absolutely not."
jokes.setup: Mac has established a checklist for the kidnapping; now assessing contact
jokes.punchline: Mac asks 'Have you touched them yet?' — another specific check-in that implies Mac has a mental protocol for child kidnapping situations
jokes.explanation: Excellent continuation. 'Have you touched them yet?' as the next logical question in Mac's protocol — and Dennis's emphatic 'Absolutely not' as if following the protocol correctly — is very dark and very funny. Dennis being proud of correctly not touching them is a perfect detail.

jokes.text: "What is she, some cheap tramp... huh?" Frank on the phone, then immediately "Oh, no."
jokes.setup: Frank can apparently hear the confrontation escalating on Dennis's end of the phone
jokes.punchline: Frank's characterization of the arriving wife as 'some cheap tramp' — without any information — followed by the dawning realization this is bad
jokes.explanation: Minor Frank character beat. 'Cheap tramp' as his default characterization is Frank-specific, but it's a small moment.

jokes.text: "Hi. Uh, I understand that. Listen, I wanted to say I'm really sorry about the kids. I tell you what, I did not mean to kidnap them. That was all... that was all this guy."
jokes.setup: Bill's wife confronts the scene; Dee tries to defuse it
jokes.punchline: Dee's 'apology' immediately shifts blame to Bill for the kidnapping — 'that was all this guy' — a completely transparent deflection delivered as if it's diplomatic
jokes.explanation: Good Dee moment — she immediately covers her own ass while pretending to apologize. 'That was all this guy' is a funny deflection line.

jokes.text: "Actually, I loaned it to both of you ladies..." — Bill revealing he gave cars to both his wife AND his mistress
jokes.setup: Bill's wife claims the car; Dee also claims the car; Bill awkwardly tries to explain
jokes.punchline: He gave cars to both of them — revealing he is somehow an even more spectacular failure than previously established
jokes.explanation: Good escalation reveal. The 'both of you ladies' landing as the explanation is well-structured. The chaos erupting (wife and mistress both furious) is a satisfying comedy escalation.

jokes.text: "What? How many mistresses do you have?" / "Mistress? I'm his wife."
jokes.setup: Dee assumes the arriving woman is another mistress
jokes.punchline: She's the wife — Dee has been operating on the wrong assumption about the entire power dynamic of the scene
jokes.explanation: Good quick reversal. 'What? How many mistresses do you have?' as a resigned question, followed by the corrective 'I'm his wife,' is efficiently structured.

jokes.text: "How much does he owe you?" / "What?" / "How much does he owe you, whore? How much does he owe you for the sex?" / "I'm not a prostitute." / "Oh, well, congratulations. You're the only woman he didn't have to pay to sleep with. You must be very proud of yourself."
jokes.setup: Bill's wife assumes Dee is a paid prostitute
jokes.punchline: When Dee clarifies she's not a prostitute, the wife's response — 'congratulations, you're the only one' — makes it WORSE, implying Bill paid all his other women and Dee did it for free
jokes.explanation: One of the absolute best jokes in the episode. The structure is exceptional: the setup (you're a prostitute) is bad enough, but the reversal (you're the ONLY one who wasn't paid) is devastating and funnier than the original insult. 'You must be very proud of yourself' as a deadpan kicker makes it land perfectly. It's a double-inversion that's both dark and structurally elegant. Dee being obliterated by this is perfect character payoff for her smug car-bragging earlier.

jokes.text: "The gravity of my situation just set in." Dee's quiet, ruined talking head after the confrontation
jokes.setup: Dee has just been comprehensively destroyed by Bill's wife
jokes.punchline: Her understated 'the gravity of my situation just set in' — delivered with quiet devastation — is funnier than any big reaction would be
jokes.explanation: Good understated reaction beat. The economy is perfect — one sentence does all the work. The camera presumably sitting on Dee's quietly crushed face before the cut is the visual version of this joke.

jokes.text: "What's in the fanny pack?" / "Oh, check this out, Mac and Dennis." Uncle Jack reveals a fanny pack full of something, then does a 'victory dance'
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack appears at the law office where Dennis is meeting about his divorce
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack has a fanny pack he's been carrying mysteriously and reveals it with theatrical pride — combined with a 'little victory dance' — the absurdity of this small-handed lawyer having a fanny pack victory routine
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag with Uncle Jack's fanny pack and victory dance. The surprise of the dance in a legal setting is funny, though without seeing what's in the pack, the transcript version loses some impact. Rewatch bonus for the visual.

jokes.text: "Just a little victory dance." Uncle Jack doing a victory dance with his fanny pack at the divorce
jokes.setup: Mac arrives at the divorce proceedings; Uncle Jack has a fanny pack
jokes.punchline: He explains the fanny pack contains materials for 'a little victory dance' — having pre-planned a celebration and brought props, which he then appears to perform
jokes.explanation: Uncle Jack pre-packing a victory dance kit in a fanny pack is very funny. The specificity of the fanny pack and the premeditation of a 'little victory dance' tells you everything about this character. 'No.' as the response to 'Thought maybe we could hang out later' is a good button.

jokes.text: "Oh, Mr. Reynolds. Oh, uh, I'm sorry, what are you doing here?" / "Well, when I heard you were getting divorced, I felt compelled to involve myself." / "I'm sorry, how would you have heard that?"
jokes.setup: Dennis arrives for his divorce consultation and finds his opposing lawyer already there
jokes.punchline: The lawyer 'felt compelled to involve himself' in a stranger's divorce — immediately raising the question of how he heard and why he'd involve himself at all
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for a bigger reveal. 'Felt compelled to involve myself' is a funny phrase — the phrasing suggests compulsion without reason.

jokes.text: "...listening to you drunkenly explain all that at 3:00 a.m. I enjoyed it so much, that I tracked down Maureen here and I offered her my services... pro bono, of course."
jokes.setup: Dennis asks how the lawyer heard about the divorce
jokes.punchline: He overheard Dennis's drunk 3 AM breakdown, enjoyed it enough to track down Maureen and offer to represent her for free — the detail that he tracked her down is the disturbing escalation
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke — the lawyer tracking down Maureen after enjoying Dennis's humiliation is a strange, motivated villainy that sets up Dennis's legal peril nicely. 'Pro bono, of course' as a dignified addition to what is essentially stalking is funny.

jokes.text: "Aw... Boy, the old place, huh?" Dennis and Mac nostalgic at the bar they were just at
jokes.setup: They return to Paddy's Pub during the legal proceedings
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Mac act nostalgic about 'the old place' — a bar they were literally just at — treating it like a sentimental homecoming
jokes.explanation: Good quick gag. The characters treating their own bar like it's a place they haven't seen in years undercuts the drama of the divorce proceedings with absurd nostalgia.

jokes.text: "I use shea butter. Assorted lanolin products." / "Oh, I'm serious, you could be a hand model. You've got the goods."
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack's small hands insecurity has been running throughout; now they're in the meeting
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack begins complimenting Mac's hands and suggesting he has what it takes to be a hand model — the small hands obsession escalates to Uncle Jack admiring other people's hands
jokes.explanation: Excellent running gag payoff. Uncle Jack's hand fixation evolving from insecurity to connoisseurship — now evaluating other people's hands — is a great character escalation. 'You've got the goods' as hand-model praise from a small-handed lawyer in the middle of legal proceedings is very funny. The shea butter detail is a nice absurd addition.

jokes.text: "That was quick, guys. Open and shut case, Dennis. / Did you get the apartment back? / I sure did. / You did? / And you also acquired Ms. Ponderosa's debt. / What? You're in debt?"
jokes.setup: Dennis confidently expects good news from Uncle Jack
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack got him the apartment back AND Maureen's debt — the 'win' comes with a devastating financial attachment
jokes.explanation: Good reversal structure. The 'open and shut case' raising Dennis's hopes only to deliver the debt twist is well-executed. Dennis's 'You did?' as hopeful confirmation before the shoe drops is good structural setup.

jokes.text: "About 90K." Dennis's debt revelation
jokes.setup: Dennis asks how much debt he's acquired
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack delivers '90K' with the same energy as a small inconvenience — $90,000 of debt as a minor footnote to the apartment win
jokes.explanation: The casualness of delivering $90,000 in debt as a small aside is a good deadpan moment. The specific number (not 'a lot' but exactly 90K) makes it funnier. The subsequent alimony revelation compounds the disaster.

jokes.text: "...you assumed her debt in addition to the alimony payments, of course." / "Wait a second... so I got to pay alimony payments?" / "Uncle Jack, what the hell?!" / "I froze up." / "He's great." — Maureen delighted
jokes.setup: Dennis expects Uncle Jack to have protected him
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack 'froze up' against the opposing lawyer — his entire contribution was getting Dennis alimony obligations AND Maureen's debt; Maureen is delighted and calls the other lawyer 'great'
jokes.explanation: Very satisfying structural payoff — Uncle Jack's complete failure, explained only as 'I froze up,' is the perfect anticlimactic explanation after all his confidence. Maureen's delighted 'He's great' about the opposing lawyer while Dennis is ruined is a good button.

jokes.text: "Hey, Mac, would you mind taking a shot of the three of us for the Web site. / Come on, Dennis. / And would it be okay if you put your hands on top of mine? Like they're my hands? / Sure, yeah. / Like that? / Yes. / Okay. / That looks like my hands. / For the Web site. / We're lawyers."
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack wants a website photo; he previously wanted his hands excluded
jokes.punchline: He's found a workaround: having Mac put his hands on top of Uncle Jack's, so it looks like Uncle Jack has normal-sized hands. The final 'We're lawyers' as a caption suggestion is a beautiful non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of Always Sunny's finest character-based gags. Everything earned over the entire episode pays off: Uncle Jack's small hands insecurity, his interest in Mac's hands, the website photo — all converge in the perfect absurd solution of using Mac's hands as a hand double. 'Like they're my hands?' / 'Yes.' is immaculately structured. And then 'We're lawyers.' as the proposed caption — delivered with complete earnestness — is a transcendent punchline. This is the show at its very best: a ridiculous running gag constructed with the architecture of a classic comic scene.

tmdb_overview: Marital bliss turns into business, as the gang experiences the emotional and economic hardships of divorce.
